decks.title: Organisms and Populations — Part 1: Population attributes and growth
goals: Define population density and describe ways of measuring it
Calculate natality, mortality and change in population size; interpret sex ratio and age pyramids
Explain exponential and logistic growth with equations and graphs, and carrying capacity

slides.heading: Populations
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the attributes of a population and how populations grow.

visual.alt: Flow from population attributes to change in size to growth models to carrying capacity

slides.narration: A population is a group of individuals of one species living in a defined area at the same time. Unlike a single organism, a population has a birth rate, a death rate, a sex ratio and an age structure, and these decide how it grows.

slides.heading: Population attributes
slides.body_md: A population has attributes that an individual does not.

rows: Number of individuals per unit area or volume
Births per individual per unit time
Deaths per individual per unit time
Individuals entering from or leaving to other habitats
Proportions of pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive individuals

visual.alt: Table of population attributes

slides.narration: An individual is born and dies, but a population has birth and death rates. An individual is male or female, but a population has a sex ratio. These features describe the population as a whole.

slides.heading: Measuring population density
slides.body_md: Counting every individual is often impossible, so ecologists use the method that suits the organism.

rows: Large, easily seen animals, such as a herd in a reserve
Plants and slow-moving animals: count in sample squares and scale up
When numbers mislead, e.g. one huge banyan tree versus many small herbs
Pug marks and faecal pellets of tigers
Mobile animals such as fish or insects

visual.alt: Table of methods of measuring population density

slides.narration: Sometimes the relative density is enough, such as the number of fish caught per trap. In a forest, one large tree may matter more than two hundred small plants, so percentage cover or biomass gives a truer picture than a simple count.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: estimating density and size
slides.body_md: (i) Five 1 m² quadrats in a meadow held 12, 9, 15, 8, 11 plants of a herb. Find the density. (ii) In a pond, 60 fish were caught, marked and released; later 50 were caught, of which 12 were marked. Estimate the fish population.
bullets: (i) Density $= \dfrac{12 + 9 + 15 + 8 + 11}{5\ \text{m}^{2}} = 11$ plants per m².
(ii) $N = \dfrac{\text{marked} \times \text{caught}}{\text{recaptured}} = \dfrac{60 \times 50}{12} = 250$ fish.

visual.alt: Worked table: 11 plants per square metre; about 250 fish

slides.narration: Averaging over several quadrats smooths out patchiness. In mark and recapture, the fraction of marked fish in the second catch is taken to equal the fraction of the whole population that was marked.

slides.heading: What changes population density
slides.body_md: Density changes through four processes: **natality (B)** and **immigration (I)** increase it; **mortality (D)** and **emigration (E)** decrease it. Over a time interval: **N(t+1) = N(t) + [(B + I) − (D + E)]**.

slides.narration: Usually births and deaths are the most important. Immigration may matter when a new habitat is being colonised, and emigration when a population becomes crowded.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: rates and change in numbers
slides.body_md: (i) A pond had 50 water lilies last year; 15 new plants were added by reproduction. (ii) In a lab, 6 of 80 beetles died in a week. Find each rate. (iii) A deer population of 500 has 60 births, 14 immigrants, 40 deaths and 9 emigrants in a year. Find N next year.
bullets: (i) Birth rate $= \dfrac{15}{50} = 0.3$ per plant per year.
(ii) Death rate $= \dfrac{6}{80} = 0.075$ per beetle per week.

visual.alt: Worked table: birth rate 0.3; death rate 0.075; 525 deer

slides.narration: Rates are always per individual per unit time, so divide the number of births or deaths by the starting population. For the change in numbers, add the gains and subtract the losses.

slides.heading: Sex ratio and carrying capacity
slides.body_md: The **sex ratio** (for example 60 percent females and 40 percent males) affects how many offspring can be produced. Every habitat has limited resources and can support only a certain maximum number: its **carrying capacity (K)**.

rows: Proportion of females to males in a population
Maximum population a habitat can support with its resources
Birth rate minus death rate per individual: Norway rat 0.015, flour beetle 0.12, India (1981) 0.0205

visual.alt: Table of sex ratio, carrying capacity and r

slides.narration: Because only females bear young, a population with more females can grow faster. But no population can grow for ever; food, space and other resources set a ceiling, the carrying capacity.

slides.heading: Quick check: density
slides.body_md: Which is the best way to measure the population of tigers in a large reserve?
slides.narration: Quick check. Tigers are rarely seen, but they leave signs.

slides.heading: Exponential and logistic growth
slides.body_md: With **unlimited resources**, growth is **exponential**: dN/dt = **rN**, giving a **J-shaped** curve, N_t = N₀e^{rt}. With **limited resources**, growth is **logistic** (Verhulst–Pearl): dN/dt = **rN(K − N)/K**, giving an **S-shaped (sigmoid)** curve that levels off at **K**.

slides.narration: In the J curve, numbers rise faster and faster. In the S curve, a lag phase is followed by rapid growth, then growth slows as resources run short, and the population settles near the carrying capacity. The logistic model is more realistic.

slides.heading: Phases of the logistic curve
slides.body_md: The sigmoid curve has four phases.

rows: Few individuals; slow growth while they adjust
Rapid growth with plenty of resources
Growth slows as competition for resources rises
Population steady at the carrying capacity K

visual.alt: Table of the phases of logistic growth

slides.narration: As N approaches K, the term K minus N over K approaches zero, so the growth rate falls towards zero. That is why the S curve flattens out at the carrying capacity.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: doubling time and logistic slowing
slides.body_md: For the flour beetle, r = 0.12 per day. Find the doubling time if growth were exponential. Then compare dN/dt at N = 100 and at N = 900 when K = 1000.
bullets: Doubling time $= \dfrac{\ln 2}{r} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.12} \approx 5.8$ days.

visual.alt: Worked table: growth is fastest at half of K

slides.narration: With no limits, the beetles would double in under six days. In the logistic model, growth is slow when there are few beetles and again when the population nears its carrying capacity; it is fastest at about half of K.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Density measured by total count, quadrats, percentage cover or biomass, indirect signs, mark and recapture.
Natality and immigration increase N; mortality and emigration decrease it: N(t+1) = N(t) + [(B + I) − (D + E)].
Age pyramids: expanding, stable, declining; sex ratio; carrying capacity K.
Exponential: dN/dt = rN, J-shaped. Logistic: dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K, S-shaped, levels at K.
r: Norway rat 0.015, flour beetle 0.12, India (1981) 0.0205.

visual.alt: Summary table of growth models

slides.narration: To recap: populations have density, rates, sex ratios and age structures. They grow exponentially when resources are unlimited, but in nature growth is logistic and levels off at the carrying capacity.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **N(t+1)** equation and use it in calculations.
Give rates **per individual per unit time**.
Draw **J and S curves** on one graph, labelling **K**.
Name the **three pyramid shapes** and what each predicts.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Use the equation for change in numbers. Express rates per individual. Draw the two growth curves together and label the carrying capacity. And learn the three shapes of age pyramid.

decks.title: Organisms and Populations — Part 2: Life history and population interactions
goals: Explain life history variation and reproductive fitness
Describe mutualism and competition, including interference competition, competitive release and Gause’s principle
Describe predation and anti-predator adaptations, parasitism, commensalism and amensalism

slides.heading: Living together
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how organisms maximise reproductive fitness, and how populations of different species interact.

visual.alt: Flow from life history to the main population interactions

slides.narration: Every species tries to leave as many surviving offspring as possible, and no species lives alone. Its populations help, harm, or ignore populations of other species living nearby.

slides.heading: Life history variation
slides.body_md: Populations evolve to maximise **reproductive fitness (Darwinian fitness)**, a high r, in the habitat where they live.

rows: Breed only once in a lifetime

visual.alt: Table of life history patterns

slides.narration: Ecologists suggest that life-history traits evolve under the limits set by the abiotic and biotic surroundings. A species may put all its energy into one huge breeding event, like a salmon, or spread it over many seasons, like most mammals.

slides.heading: Population interactions
slides.body_md: Interactions between two species can be beneficial (+), harmful (−) or neutral (0) to each.

visual.alt: Table of population interactions with plus, minus and zero signs

slides.narration: In mutualism both gain, and in competition both lose. In predation and parasitism one gains at the other’s expense. In commensalism one gains while the other is unaffected, and in amensalism one is harmed while the other is unaffected.

slides.heading: Mutualism
slides.body_md: In **mutualism** both species benefit.

rows: Fungus gives shelter and water; alga or cyanobacterium makes food
Fungus absorbs nutrients for the plant; plant supplies carbohydrates
Wasp pollinates the fig while laying eggs; fig seeds feed the wasp larvae (each fig species has its own wasp partner)
Petal resembles a female bee; the male “pseudocopulates” and carries pollen (sexual deceit)

visual.alt: Table of examples of mutualism

slides.narration: Plants need animals to pollinate flowers and disperse seeds, and they reward them with nectar, pollen or fruit. Some partnerships are so close that each species depends on the other, like a fig and its wasp. The Ophrys orchid even tricks bees into pollinating it.

slides.heading: Competition
slides.body_md: **Competition** harms both species. It occurs between closely related species, but also between unrelated ones for the same resource; resources need not be limiting — in **interference competition**, one species reduces the feeding efficiency of another.

rows: Flamingoes and fishes in South American lakes
Became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced, which were better at browsing
Larger Balanus excluded Chthamalus from the lower rocks; when Balanus was removed, Chthamalus spread there — competitive release

visual.alt: Table of examples of competition

slides.narration: Competitive release shows that a species confined to a small area can expand when a superior competitor is removed. Joseph Connell showed this with barnacles on Scottish rocky shores.

slides.heading: Gause’s competitive exclusion principle
slides.body_md: **Gause’s principle**: two closely related species competing for the **same limiting resources** cannot coexist indefinitely; the **competitively inferior** one is eventually **eliminated**. Gause showed this with two species of **Paramecium**.

slides.narration: Grown alone, each species of Paramecium reaches its own carrying capacity. Grown together on the same food, one keeps increasing while the other rises at first and then declines and disappears.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading the competition model
slides.body_md: In the model, species 2 grown with species 1 peaks on day 6 and then declines. Read the peak and the final numbers, and state the principle shown.
bullets: Species 2 alone reaches about **160**; with species 1 it peaks at only about **38** (day 6) and falls to **0** by day 24.
Species 1 reaches about **200** either way.
**Competitive exclusion**: the inferior competitor is eliminated.

visual.alt: Worked table: species 2 falls to 0 when grown with species 1

slides.narration: Comparing the two panels shows the effect of competition. Species 2 does well alone, but sharing food with a better competitor drives it out. This is what Gause found with Paramecium.

slides.heading: Resource partitioning
slides.body_md: Competing species can **coexist** by **resource partitioning**: using the same resource in different ways, places or times.

rows: Five warbler species on one tree (MacArthur)
Feed in different parts of the branches with different foraging activities
Feed at different heights or times

visual.alt: Table of examples of resource partitioning

slides.narration: Robert MacArthur found five closely related warblers living on the same tree. They avoided competition and coexisted because each fed in a different part of the tree in a different way.

slides.heading: Quick check: Gause
slides.body_md: What does Gause’s competitive exclusion principle state?
slides.narration: Quick check. Can two species share exactly the same limiting resources for ever?

slides.heading: Predation and anti-predator defences
slides.body_md: **Predators** transfer energy to higher trophic levels, **keep prey populations in check** and help **maintain species diversity**. Prey have evolved defences.

rows: Some insects and frogs blend with their background
Monarch butterfly stores a poison from the weed it ate as a caterpillar
Calotropis makes cardiac glycosides; nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium deter herbivores

visual.alt: Table of anti-predator defences

slides.narration: When the prickly pear cactus spread over millions of hectares in Australia, it was controlled only by bringing in a moth that eats it. When the starfish Pisaster was removed from a rocky shore, more than ten species of invertebrates disappeared within a year, because one prey species took over.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a keystone predator
slides.body_md: On an American rocky shore, removal of the predatory starfish Pisaster reduced the number of invertebrate species from about 15 to 5 within a year (illustrative figures). What percentage of species was lost, and why?
bullets: Loss $= \dfrac{10}{15} \times 100 = 66.7$ percent.
Without the predator, **one prey species out-competed the others** for space, so diversity fell.

visual.alt: Worked table: 66.7 percent of species lost

slides.narration: Predators can increase diversity by preventing any one prey species from becoming dominant. Remove the predator, and competition among prey eliminates many species.

slides.heading: Parasitism
slides.body_md: Parasites live on or in a **host**, gaining food and shelter and harming it. Many are **host-specific** and have special **adaptations**: loss of unnecessary sense organs, **adhesive organs or suckers**, loss of the digestive system, and **high reproductive capacity**; many need **intermediate hosts** (the human liver fluke uses a snail and a fish).

rows: Lice on humans, ticks on dogs, copepods on marine fish, Cuscuta on hedge plants
Cuckoo (koel) lays eggs in the nest of a crow, which rears its young; the eggs mimic the host’s in size and colour

visual.alt: Table of types of parasites with examples

slides.narration: Endoparasites have the simplest bodies, since they live surrounded by food. The cuckoo’s eggs resemble the crow’s, which reduces the chance that the host will detect and throw them out.

slides.heading: Commensalism and amensalism
slides.body_md: In **commensalism** one species benefits and the other is **neither harmed nor benefited**; in **amensalism** one is **harmed** and the other **unaffected**.

rows: Orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch
Barnacles on the back of a whale
Cattle egrets feeding on insects stirred up by grazing cattle
Clown fish living among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone
Penicillium secretes penicillin, which harms bacteria, while the mould is unaffected

visual.alt: Table of examples of commensalism and amensalism

slides.narration: The clown fish gains protection among the anemone’s stinging tentacles, and the anemone does not seem to gain anything. In amensalism, a mould releases a chemical that harms nearby bacteria without any effect on itself.

slides.heading: Quick check: brood parasites
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the cuckoo.
slides.narration: Quick check. Why do the cuckoo’s eggs look like the crow’s?

slides.heading: Quick check: commensalism
slides.body_md: Which pair shows commensalism?
slides.narration: Quick check. One gains and the other is unaffected.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Life history: maximise reproductive fitness; breed once (salmon, bamboo) or many times; many small or few large offspring.
Mutualism: lichens, mycorrhizae, fig and wasp, Ophrys (sexual deceit).
Competition: flamingoes and fish, Abingdon tortoise, interference; competitive release (Connell); Gause’s principle; resource partitioning (MacArthur).
Predation: control of prey (prickly pear), diversity (Pisaster); defences: camouflage, Monarch, thorns, Calotropis.
Parasitism (ecto-, endo-, brood); commensalism (orchid, barnacles, egret, clown fish); amensalism (Penicillium).

visual.alt: Summary table of interactions and signs

slides.narration: To recap: life histories are shaped to maximise reproductive fitness. Species interact as mutualists, competitors, predators, parasites, commensals or amensals, and these interactions shape communities.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give each interaction with its **signs** and a **named example**.
State **Gause’s principle** and give **Connell’s** and **MacArthur’s** examples.
List **three adaptations** of parasites and **three** anti-predator defences.
Distinguish **ecto-, endo- and brood** parasites.
slides.narration: Exam tips. For each interaction, give the signs and an example. Learn Gause’s principle with the barnacle and warbler examples. List adaptations of parasites and defences of prey. And keep the three kinds of parasite apart.

sections.heading: 1. Population attributes
sections.body_md:
A **population** is a group of individuals of a species living in a well-defined geographical area, sharing or competing for similar resources and potentially interbreeding. A population has attributes that individual organisms do not.

**Population density (N)** — the number of individuals per unit area or volume. It may be measured by: a **total count** (large, visible animals); **quadrats** (plants; count in sample squares); **percentage cover** or **biomass** when a simple count is misleading (a single huge banyan tree versus 200 carrot-grass plants); **relative density** (fish caught per trap); **indirect signs** such as **pug marks and faecal pellets** (tiger census); and **mark–recapture**: N = (number marked × number in second catch) ÷ number recaptured marked (for example, 60 marked, 50 caught, 12 recaptured → about 250).

**Natality** is the number of births during a given period that are added to the initial density; the **birth rate** is expressed per individual per unit time (for example 0.3 per plant per year). **Mortality** is the number of deaths; the **death rate** is per individual per unit time (for example 0.075). **Immigration** is the number of individuals of the same species that come into the habitat from elsewhere; **emigration** the number that leave. Hence
**N(t+1) = N(t) + [(B + I) − (D + E)]**.

**Sex ratio** is the proportion of females to males (for example 60 percent female, 40 percent male).

**Age structure:** plotted as an **age pyramid** of pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive individuals: **expanding** (triangular, broad base — growing), **stable** (bell-shaped) and **declining** (urn-shaped).

**Carrying capacity (K)** — the maximum number of individuals of a species that a habitat can support, set by its limited resources.

key_terms.definition_md: Number of individuals per unit area or volume.
Births per individual per unit time.
Deaths per individual per unit time.
Maximum population a habitat can support.

sections.heading: 2. Population growth
sections.body_md:
**Exponential growth:** when resources are **unlimited**, each species can realise its full innate potential to grow. If the per-capita birth rate is b and death rate d, the **intrinsic rate of natural increase** is **r = b − d**, and
**dN/dt = rN**, integrating to **N_t = N₀e^{rt}**.
The graph of N against t is **J-shaped**. Values of r: Norway rat **0.015**, flour beetle **0.12**, human population of India in 1981 **0.0205**. Doubling time = ln 2 ÷ r.

**Logistic growth:** no population has unlimited resources; competition for food and space leads to survival of the fittest. A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows a **lag phase**, then **acceleration**, then **deceleration**, and finally an **asymptote** when density reaches the **carrying capacity K**. This **sigmoid (S-shaped)** curve is the **Verhulst–Pearl logistic growth** model:
**dN/dt = rN (K − N)/K**.
As N approaches K, (K − N)/K approaches zero, so growth slows and stops. Since resources for most animal populations are finite, the logistic model is considered **more realistic**.

key_terms.definition_md: Per-capita birth rate minus death rate.
Growth with unlimited resources: dN/dt = rN; J-shaped.
Growth limited by K: dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K; S-shaped.

sections.heading: 3. Life history variation
sections.body_md:
Populations evolve to **maximise their reproductive fitness**, also called **Darwinian fitness (high r value)**, in the habitat in which they live. Under a particular set of selection pressures, organisms evolve towards the most efficient reproductive strategy.
- Some organisms **breed only once** in their lifetime (**Pacific salmon fish, bamboo**); others **breed many times** (most **birds and mammals**).
- Some produce a **large number of small-sized offspring** (**oysters, pelagic fishes**); others produce a **small number of large-sized offspring** (**birds, mammals**).
Ecologists suggest that **life-history traits** of organisms have evolved in relation to the **constraints imposed by the abiotic and biotic components** of the habitat.

key_terms.definition_md: Ability to leave surviving offspring; a high r.
Pattern of growth, reproduction and survival over a lifetime.

sections.heading: 4. Mutualism and competition
sections.body_md:
**Population interactions** (+ beneficial, − detrimental, 0 neutral): mutualism (+, +), competition (−, −), predation (+, −), parasitism (+, −), commensalism (+, 0), amensalism (−, 0).

**Mutualism:** both species benefit. **Lichens** — a fungus and a photosynthesising alga or cyanobacterium. **Mycorrhizae** — fungi and roots of higher plants: the fungus helps absorb nutrients; the plant provides carbohydrates. **Plant–animal mutualism**: plants reward pollinators and seed dispersers with nectar, pollen or fruit. Every **fig species** is pollinated only by its partner **wasp species**; the female wasp uses the fruit as an egg-laying site and pollinates the fig inflorescence, and the developing seeds feed its larvae. The Mediterranean orchid ***Ophrys*** uses **sexual deceit**: one petal resembles the female of a bee species, and the male “pseudocopulates” with it and transfers pollen.

**Competition:** both species are harmed. It is commonly between closely related species competing for the same limited resources, but this is not always so: **flamingoes and resident fishes** in some shallow South American lakes compete for **zooplankton**. Resources need not be limiting: in **interference competition**, the feeding efficiency of one species may be reduced by the interfering and inhibitory presence of the other. The **Abingdon tortoise** of the Galapagos became extinct within a decade after **goats** were introduced, owing to the goats’ greater browsing efficiency.
- **Competitive release:** a species whose distribution is restricted by a superior competitor **expands dramatically** when the competitor is removed. **Connell** showed that on the rocky sea coasts of **Scotland**, the larger and competitively superior barnacle ***Balanus*** dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller ***Chthamalus***.
- **Gause’s competitive exclusion principle:** two closely related species competing for the same resources **cannot coexist indefinitely**; the competitively inferior one will eventually be **eliminated** (shown with two species of *Paramecium*).
- **Resource partitioning:** **MacArthur** showed that **five closely related species of warblers** on the same tree avoided competition and coexisted because of differences in their **foraging activities**.

key_terms.definition_md: One species reduces the feeding efficiency of another even when resources are not limiting.
Expansion of a species when a superior competitor is removed.
Two species with identical requirements cannot coexist indefinitely.

sections.heading: 5. Predation, parasitism, commensalism and amensalism
sections.body_md:
**Predation:** nature’s way of **transferring energy** fixed by plants to higher trophic levels. Predators keep **prey populations under control** — the **prickly pear cactus** introduced into Australia spread over millions of hectares until a cactus-feeding **moth** was introduced. Predators help **maintain species diversity** by reducing competition among prey: when the starfish ***Pisaster*** was removed from an American intertidal community, **more than 10 species of invertebrates** became extinct within a year owing to interspecific competition. Prudent predators avoid over-exploiting their prey.
**Anti-predator defences:** **camouflage (cryptic colouration)** in some insects and frogs; the **Monarch butterfly** is distasteful because of a chemical it acquires by feeding on a poisonous weed as a caterpillar; **thorns** (Acacia, cactus); **chemicals** — ***Calotropis*** produces highly poisonous **cardiac glycosides**; nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium are produced as defences against grazers and browsers.

**Parasitism:** the parasite gains food and shelter at the host’s expense. Many parasites are **host-specific** and have evolved adaptations: **loss of unnecessary sense organs**, **adhesive organs or suckers**, **loss of the digestive system**, and **high reproductive capacity**. Life cycles are often complex, with **intermediate hosts** — the **human liver fluke** depends on a **snail** and a **fish**; the malaria parasite needs a **mosquito**. Parasites may reduce host survival, growth and reproduction and make the host more vulnerable to predators.
- **Ectoparasites** feed on the external surface: **lice** on humans, **ticks** on dogs, **copepods** on marine fish; ***Cuscuta*** on hedge plants (it has lost its chlorophyll and leaves).
- **Endoparasites** live inside the host: tapeworm, liver fluke, *Plasmodium*; they have simplified morphology and high reproductive potential.
- **Brood parasitism:** the **cuckoo (koel)** lays eggs in the nest of its host, the **crow**, which incubates them; the parasitic eggs **resemble the host’s eggs** in size and colour, reducing the chance that the host detects and ejects them.

**Commensalism:** one species benefits; the other is neither harmed nor benefited — an **orchid** growing as an epiphyte on a **mango** branch; **barnacles** on the back of a **whale**; **cattle egrets** foraging near grazing **cattle**, which stir up insects; **sea anemone and clown fish** (the fish gains protection from predators among the stinging tentacles).

**Amensalism:** one species is harmed and the other is unaffected — for example ***Penicillium*** secretes penicillin, which inhibits bacteria.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving rates as totals instead of per individual per unit time.
- Writing dN/dt = rN for logistic growth (logistic is rN(K − N)/K).
- Calling a declining population’s pyramid triangular (it is urn-shaped).
- Saying competition occurs only when resources are limiting (interference competition does not need this).
- Calling Cuscuta an endoparasite (it is an ectoparasite).
- Mixing up commensalism (+, 0) and amensalism (−, 0).

- 1-mark subparts: an attribute, a value of r, an example of an interaction, a parasite type.
- 2–3-mark questions: birth and death rates; N(t+1); age pyramids; Gause’s principle; competitive release; parasite adaptations.
- 5-mark questions in parts: growth models with graphs and equations; population interactions with examples.

questions.stem_md: Forest officials want to estimate the number of tigers in a large reserve where tigers are rarely seen. Which method is most practical?

options.text_md: Counting every tiger seen from a jeep
Placing 1 m² quadrats across the reserve
Measuring the percentage cover of tigers
Counting pug marks and faecal pellets

questions.solution_md: Indirect signs give a reliable relative estimate for elusive animals — option (d).

questions.stem_md: One huge banyan tree and 200 small weeds grow in a plot. Why is a simple count of plants a poor measure of their relative importance?

options.text_md: Numbers ignore size; percentage cover or biomass reflects the banyan’s far larger share.
Plants can never be counted.
Weeds are not living organisms.
The banyan should be counted as 200 plants.

questions.solution_md: When individuals differ greatly in size, cover or biomass is more meaningful — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In ecology, natality refers to

options.text_md: the number of individuals entering from another habitat
the number of births in a population during a given period, added to the initial density
the number of deaths in a given period
the ratio of females to males

questions.solution_md: Natality is births; immigration is entry from outside — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A new pond forms after heavy rain, and within weeks it holds frogs that arrived from nearby ponds. Which process mainly increased the frog population at first?

options.text_md: Immigration
Natality
Emigration
Mortality

questions.solution_md: When a new habitat is colonised, immigration is the main source of individuals — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An age pyramid with a narrow base of pre-reproductive individuals and a wider middle (urn-shaped) indicates a population that is

options.text_md: expanding rapidly
stable
declining
at zero age

questions.solution_md: Few young individuals mean future decline — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Two deer herds have the same size, but herd A is 70 percent female and herd B 30 percent female. Other things being equal, which herd can produce more fawns next season, and why?

options.text_md: Herd A, because more females can bear young
Herd B, because males produce the young
Both equally, because sex ratio does not affect births
Neither, because deer breed only once

questions.solution_md: Sex ratio affects natality; more females give more births — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An urn-shaped age pyramid indicates a rapidly growing population.

**Reason (R):** Urn-shaped pyramids have a broad base of pre-reproductive individuals.

Choose the correct option.

Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: an urn shape has a narrow base and indicates a declining population — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A pond had 40 water hyacinth plants last year; 14 new plants were added by reproduction. What is the birth rate per plant per year?
questions.solution_md: Birth rate $= \dfrac{14}{40} = 0.35$ per plant per year.

questions.stem_md: In a culture of 120 fruit flies, 9 died during a week. What is the death rate per fly per week?
questions.solution_md: Death rate $= \dfrac{9}{120} = 0.075$ per fly per week.

questions.stem_md: A population of 2400 rabbits has 310 births, 45 immigrants, 260 deaths and 95 emigrants in a year. What is its size at the end of the year?
In a lake, 40 fish were caught, tagged and released. A week later 75 fish were caught, of which 10 carried tags. Estimate the fish population.
Six quadrats, each 0.25 m², placed in a grassland held 6, 4, 7, 3, 5, 5 dandelion plants. What is the density of dandelions per square metre?
questions.solution_md: Total $= 30$ plants in $6 \times 0.25 = 1.5$ m²; density $= \dfrac{30}{1.5} = 20$ per m².

questions.stem_md: Name four attributes that a population has but an individual organism does not.

answer.model_answer_md: A population has a **population density**, a **birth rate (natality)** and a **death rate (mortality)** expressed per individual, a **sex ratio**, and an **age structure (age pyramid)**. An individual is born, dies and is male or female, but has none of these rates or ratios.

questions.solution_md: Four attributes.

questions.stem_md: Age pyramids of three countries are: X — broad base, narrow top; Y — almost equal widths of pre-reproductive and reproductive groups; Z — narrow base, wider middle. Name each shape and predict what will happen to each population.

answer.model_answer_md: X is **expanding (triangular)**: many young individuals will soon reproduce, so the population will **grow rapidly**. Y is **stable (bell-shaped)**: the young roughly replace the reproductive group, so the population stays **about the same**. Z is **declining (urn-shaped)**: too few young to replace the adults, so the population will **decrease**.

questions.solution_md: Expanding, stable, declining.

questions.stem_md: Describe three different methods of measuring population density, stating the kind of organism for which each is suitable.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Quadrats**: count individuals in sample squares and scale up — for **plants** and slow-moving animals. (ii) **Percentage cover or biomass**: for plants of very **different sizes**, where a count would mislead. (iii) **Indirect estimates** such as **pug marks and faecal pellets** — for elusive animals like **tigers**; or **mark and recapture** for mobile animals such as **fish**.

questions.solution_md: Three methods.

questions.stem_md: A population of 150 squirrels had 30 births and 18 deaths in a year, with no migration. Calculate the birth rate, death rate and r, and state whether the population is growing.

answer.model_answer_md: Birth rate b = 30 ÷ 150 = **0.2**; death rate d = 18 ÷ 150 = **0.12** (per squirrel per year). Intrinsic rate **r = b − d = 0.08**. Since r is **positive**, the population is **growing**, from 150 to **162** in the year.

questions.solution_md: Rates; r; growth.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define population density and name two methods of measuring it. [1]
(b) Write the equation for the change in population size over a time interval and explain each term. [2]
(c) A town’s population of 18 000 had 720 births, 300 deaths, 150 immigrants and 470 emigrants in a year. Calculate the population after the year and comment on the result. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Population density** is the number of individuals per unit **area or volume**; measured by **quadrats** or **mark–recapture** (also pug marks, biomass, percentage cover).

(b) **N(t+1) = N(t) + [(B + I) − (D + E)]**, where **B** = births (natality), **I** = immigrants, **D** = deaths (mortality) and **E** = emigrants in the interval; N(t) is the starting density.

(c) N = 18 000 + (720 + 150) − (300 + 470) = **18100**. The population grew slightly; births exceeded deaths, but heavy **emigration** reduced the gain.

questions.solution_md: Density; equation; calculation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In logistic growth, the growth rate falls almost to zero as the population nears the carrying capacity.

**Reason (R):** The term (K − N)/K approaches zero as N approaches K.

Choose the correct option.

Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the shrinking factor (K − N)/K explains the slowing — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The logistic growth curve levels off at the carrying capacity.

**Reason (R):** In nature, resources available to a population are unlimited.

Choose the correct option.

Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false: resources are limited, which is why growth levels off at K — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A few bacteria are placed in a large flask of fresh nutrient broth. For some hours their numbers rise faster and faster. Which growth pattern and equation describe this phase?

options.text_md: Logistic growth, dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K, at its asymptote
Zero growth, dN/dt = 0
Exponential growth, dN/dt = rN, giving a J-shaped curve
Declining growth, dN/dt = −rN

questions.solution_md: With plentiful resources, growth is exponential — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Deer introduced to an island increase rapidly at first, then more slowly, and their numbers settle around 900 for many years. What does 900 represent?

options.text_md: The intrinsic rate of natural increase
The birth rate per deer
The carrying capacity of the island for deer
The lag phase

questions.solution_md: The asymptote of logistic growth is K — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The intrinsic rate of natural increase (r) of the human population of India in 1981 was about
questions.solution_md: r for India in 1981 was 0.0205; 0.015 is the Norway rat and 0.12 the flour beetle — option (a).

questions.stem_md: If India’s population had grown exponentially with r = 0.0205 per year, how many years would it take to double? Use doubling time = ln 2 ÷ r. (One decimal place.)
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{0.693}{0.0205} \approx 33.8$ years.

questions.stem_md: For a population growing logistically with r = 0.2 per week and K = 500, what is the growth rate dN/dt when N = 250?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = 0.2 \times 250 \times \dfrac{500 - 250}{500} = 25$.

questions.stem_md: A population of 100 aphids grows exponentially with r = 0.1 per day. Using N = N₀e^{rt}, how many aphids are there after 10 days? (Take e = 2.718; nearest whole number.)
Name the four phases of a sigmoid (logistic) growth curve and state what happens in the last one.

answer.model_answer_md: The phases are the **lag phase**, the **exponential (log) phase**, the **deceleration phase** and the **asymptote**. At the asymptote, the population has reached the **carrying capacity (K)**; births and deaths balance, so numbers stay **roughly constant**.

questions.solution_md: Four phases.

questions.stem_md: Compare exponential and logistic growth with respect to resources, equation and shape of the curve.

answer.model_answer_md: **Resources:** exponential growth occurs when resources are **unlimited**; logistic growth when they are **limited**. **Equation:** exponential — **dN/dt = rN**; logistic — **dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K**, where K is the carrying capacity. **Curve:** exponential gives a **J-shaped** curve rising ever faster; logistic gives an **S-shaped (sigmoid)** curve that levels off at **K**. The logistic model is **more realistic**.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw on one graph the curves of exponential and logistic growth, labelling the carrying capacity. [2]
(b) Write the equation for each. [1]
(c) A fish population has r = 0.4 per year in a lake with K = 2000. Calculate dN/dt when N = 1000 and when N = 1900, and explain the difference. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Graph:** time on the x-axis, N on the y-axis; a **J-shaped** exponential curve rising steeply; an **S-shaped** logistic curve with lag, rapid rise, deceleration and an **asymptote** at a dashed line marked **K**.

(b) Exponential: **dN/dt = rN**; logistic: **dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K**.

(c) At N = 1000: 0.4 × 1000 × 1000/2000 = **200** per year. At N = 1900: 0.4 × 1900 × 100/2000 = **38** per year. Near K, resources are almost used up, (K − N)/K is small, and growth **slows sharply**.

questions.solution_md: Curves; equations; calculation.

questions.stem_md: Which organisms breed only once in their lifetime and then die?

options.text_md: Most birds and mammals
Oysters and pelagic fishes
Pacific salmon and bamboo
Humans and elephants

questions.solution_md: Pacific salmon and bamboo reproduce once — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Oysters release millions of tiny eggs, while elephants have one large calf every few years. These differences are best described as

options.text_md: differences in carrying capacity only
life history variations that maximise reproductive fitness in each habitat
examples of competitive exclusion
the result of brood parasitism

questions.solution_md: Each strategy maximises Darwinian fitness under its constraints — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Populations evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness, also called ______ fitness (a high r value).
questions.solution_md: Darwinian fitness.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by life history variation? Give two contrasting examples.

answer.model_answer_md: Different species have evolved different patterns of **reproduction and survival** that **maximise reproductive fitness** in their habitats. Some **breed once** (Pacific salmon, bamboo), others **breed many times** (most birds and mammals); some produce **many small offspring** (oysters), others **few large offspring** (birds and mammals).

questions.solution_md: Definition; examples.

questions.stem_md: Gause’s competitive exclusion principle states that

options.text_md: all species in a habitat compete equally
predators always eliminate their prey
two closely related species competing for the same limiting resources cannot coexist indefinitely
competition occurs only between unrelated species

questions.solution_md: The inferior competitor is eventually eliminated — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A female wasp lays eggs inside the developing fruit of a fig species and pollinates its flowers, and her larvae feed on some of the seeds. This relationship is

options.text_md: parasitism
mutualism
commensalism
amensalism

questions.solution_md: Both benefit: the fig is pollinated and the wasp gets a site and food for its young — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys has a petal that resembles a female bee. How does this help the orchid?

options.text_md: The petal stings bees that come near.
The petal produces honey for the bees.
Bees lay their eggs in the petal.
Male bees try to mate with the petal and carry pollen to other flowers.

questions.solution_md: Sexual deceit by pseudocopulation brings about pollination — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A lichen is a mutualistic association between

options.text_md: a fungus and the roots of a higher plant
a fig and a wasp
a cuckoo and a crow
a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium

questions.solution_md: Lichens are fungus–photosynthetic partner associations — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A lake has abundant zooplankton, yet a fish species feeds less efficiently whenever a large flock of flamingoes is present. What kind of competition is this?

options.text_md: Interference competition
Mutualism
Commensalism
Brood parasitism

questions.solution_md: One species reduces the feeding efficiency of another even when the resource is not limiting — option (a).

questions.stem_md: On a Scottish rocky shore, the barnacle Chthamalus is found only on high rocks. When the larger barnacle Balanus is removed from the lower rocks, Chthamalus spreads there. This shows

options.text_md: mutualism
competitive release
brood parasitism
logistic growth

questions.solution_md: Removing a superior competitor lets the inferior species expand — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The Abingdon tortoise of the Galapagos became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced to its island. What was the main reason?

options.text_md: Goats preyed on adult tortoises.
Goats were parasites of the tortoise.
Goats were mutualists that helped the tortoise.
Goats were more efficient browsers and out-competed the tortoise for food.

questions.solution_md: Interspecific competition by a superior browser — option (d).

questions.stem_md: MacArthur found five closely related warbler species living on the same tree. How did they coexist?

options.text_md: By competitive exclusion of four species
By brood parasitism
By feeding on the same insects at the same place
By resource partitioning — feeding in different parts of the tree in different ways

questions.solution_md: Differences in foraging avoided competition — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A gardener notices that her pea plants grow well in poor soil when certain fungi live in their roots. Name this association, the type of interaction, and how each partner benefits.

answer.model_answer_md: It is **mycorrhiza**, a **mutualism** (+, +). The **fungus** helps the plant **absorb nutrients**, especially phosphorus, from the soil, while the **plant** supplies the fungus with **carbohydrates** made in photosynthesis.

questions.solution_md: Mycorrhiza; mutualism.

questions.stem_md: State Gause’s competitive exclusion principle and name the organisms he used.

answer.model_answer_md: Two **closely related species** competing for the **same resources** cannot **coexist indefinitely**; the **competitively inferior** one will eventually be **eliminated**. Gause showed this with two species of the protozoan ***Paramecium*** grown together in culture.

questions.solution_md: Principle; Paramecium.

questions.stem_md: Using the examples of flamingoes and fishes, the Abingdon tortoise, and MacArthur’s warblers, explain three different aspects of competition.

answer.model_answer_md: **Flamingoes and fishes** in South American lakes compete for **zooplankton** — competition can occur between **unrelated** species. The **Abingdon tortoise** became **extinct** within a decade of **goats** being introduced, as goats browsed more efficiently — a superior competitor can **eliminate** another. **MacArthur’s warblers** coexisted on one tree by **feeding differently** — **resource partitioning** avoids competitive exclusion.

questions.solution_md: Three aspects.

questions.stem_md: In an experiment on a rocky shore, barnacle species X lives only on upper rocks and species Y on lower rocks. When Y is removed from some lower rocks, X settles and survives there; when X is removed from upper rocks, Y does not spread upwards. Interpret these results.

answer.model_answer_md: X **can** live on the lower rocks but is normally **excluded** there by **Y**, the **superior competitor** — when Y is removed, X spreads: **competitive release**. Y does **not** spread upwards when X is removed, so its upper limit is set by **physical factors** (such as drying out), not by competition with X. X’s **realised** range is therefore smaller than its **potential** range, as Connell found with *Chthamalus* and *Balanus*.

questions.solution_md: Competitive release; physical limit.

marking_scheme.step: Y excludes X below: competitive release
Y limited above by physical factors

questions.stem_md:
(a) Tabulate the six kinds of population interaction with their signs (+, −, 0). [2]
(b) Give one example each of mutualism, commensalism and amensalism. [2]
(c) What is meant by competitive release? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Mutualism +/+; competition −/−; predation +/−; parasitism +/−; commensalism +/0; amensalism −/0.**

(b) **Mutualism:** fig and fig wasp (or lichen, mycorrhiza, Ophrys and bee). **Commensalism:** orchid epiphyte on a mango branch (or barnacles on a whale, cattle egret and cattle, clown fish and sea anemone). **Amensalism:** *Penicillium* secreting penicillin that harms bacteria.

(c) **Competitive release** is the **expansion** of a species’ distribution when a **superior competitor** that restricted it is **removed** (Connell’s barnacles).

questions.solution_md: Table; examples; release.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A crow often incubates and rears the young of a koel.

**Reason (R):** The koel’s eggs resemble the crow’s in size and colour, so the crow does not detect and eject them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and egg mimicry explains why the crow rears the koel’s young (brood parasitism) — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A clown fish gains protection by living among the tentacles of a sea anemone.

**Reason (R):** Penicillium secretes a substance that inhibits bacteria.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the action of Penicillium (amensalism) does not explain the clown fish–anemone commensalism — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Cattle egrets follow grazing buffaloes and catch the insects disturbed by them; the buffaloes are not affected. This interaction is

options.text_md: commensalism
mutualism
parasitism
amensalism

questions.solution_md: One benefits, the other is unaffected — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A leafless, yellow, thread-like plant twines over a hedge and draws food from it through special roots. It is

options.text_md: an orchid, a commensal epiphyte
Cuscuta, an ectoparasite
a lichen, a mutualistic partner
Calotropis, a plant with cardiac glycosides

questions.solution_md: Cuscuta has lost chlorophyll and leaves and parasitises the host from outside — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Birds avoid eating Monarch butterflies. Why?

options.text_md: It is camouflaged against tree bark.
The butterfly is distasteful because of a chemical it acquired by feeding on a poisonous weed as a caterpillar.
It has sharp thorns.
It is too large for birds to eat.

questions.solution_md: A chemical defence acquired from its food plant — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Cattle and goats avoid browsing on Calotropis growing in abandoned fields because it produces

options.text_md: penicillin
thorns on every leaf
nectar that attracts bees
highly poisonous cardiac glycosides

questions.solution_md: Calotropis is chemically defended — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Scientists removed all the predatory starfish Pisaster from an enclosed intertidal area. Within a year more than ten invertebrate species had disappeared. Why?

options.text_md: The starfish had been feeding all the invertebrates.
Removing the starfish made the water too warm.
Without the predator, competition among prey increased and a few species eliminated the others.
The invertebrates were parasites of the starfish.

questions.solution_md: Predators can maintain diversity by limiting dominant prey — option (c).

questions.stem_md: When the prickly pear cactus spread over millions of hectares of Australian rangeland, how was it finally brought under control?

options.text_md: By introducing a cactus-feeding predator, a moth, from its natural habitat
By introducing goats that out-competed it
By planting orchids as epiphytes on it
By spraying penicillin

questions.solution_md: An introduced herbivore (predator) controlled the invasive plant — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Bacteria fail to grow around a colony of the mould Penicillium on an agar plate, while the mould is unaffected. This interaction is

options.text_md: commensalism
amensalism
mutualism
predation

questions.solution_md: One is harmed (−) and the other unaffected (0) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The human liver fluke needs two intermediate hosts to complete its life cycle: a snail and a ______.
questions.solution_md: Fish.

questions.stem_md: State two important roles of predators in nature, with an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Predators **keep prey populations in check**: the invasive **prickly pear cactus** in Australia was controlled by a cactus-feeding **moth**. (ii) Predators **maintain species diversity** by reducing competition among prey: removal of the starfish ***Pisaster*** led to the extinction of **over ten** invertebrate species. They also **transfer energy** to higher trophic levels.

questions.solution_md: Two roles.

questions.stem_md: An orchid grows on a mango branch, and barnacles grow on the back of a whale. Name the interaction in both cases, and explain why it is not parasitism.

answer.model_answer_md: Both are **commensalism** (+, 0). The **orchid** gains support and light, and the **barnacles** gain a moving home and access to food, while the **mango tree and whale** are **neither harmed nor benefited**. In parasitism the host would be **harmed** by losing food.

questions.solution_md: Commensalism; host unharmed.

questions.stem_md: Describe three special adaptations of parasites and explain the advantage of each.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Loss of unnecessary sense organs** — inside a host they are not needed, saving energy. (ii) **Adhesive organs or suckers** — to **cling** to the host and not be dislodged. (iii) **Loss of the digestive system** (in endoparasites) — they absorb **pre-digested food** from the host. Also (iv) **high reproductive capacity**, so that some offspring find new hosts despite complex life cycles.

questions.solution_md: Three adaptations.

questions.stem_md: A field has grasses, an Acacia bush, Calotropis plants and many insects. Explain three different ways in which these prey organisms might avoid being eaten.

answer.model_answer_md: **Camouflage:** some **insects** (and frogs) are **cryptically coloured** so that predators cannot easily see them. **Thorns:** the **Acacia** bears **thorns** that deter browsers. **Chemicals:** **Calotropis** produces poisonous **cardiac glycosides**, so cattle and goats avoid it; insects such as the **Monarch** become **distasteful** by storing chemicals from their food plant.

questions.solution_md: Camouflage, thorns, chemicals.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between ectoparasites and endoparasites, giving two examples of each. [2]
(b) What is brood parasitism? Explain with an example. [2]
(c) Why do many endoparasites produce enormous numbers of eggs? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Ectoparasites** feed on the **external surface** of the host — **lice** on humans, **ticks** on dogs, copepods on fish, ***Cuscuta*** on hedge plants. **Endoparasites** live **inside** the host’s body — **tapeworm**, **liver fluke**, ***Plasmodium***.

(b) In **brood parasitism**, a parasitic bird **lays its eggs in the nest of its host** and lets the host incubate them and rear the young. The **koel (cuckoo)** lays eggs in a **crow’s** nest; its eggs **resemble the crow’s** in size and colour, so the crow does not reject them.

(c) Their life cycles are **complex**, often needing **intermediate hosts**, and most eggs never reach a new host; **high reproductive capacity** ensures some do.

questions.solution_md: Ecto vs endo; brood; eggs.

questions.passage_md:
A student recorded a frog population in a closed pond (no migration) each spring.

| Year | Frogs at start | Births during year | Deaths during year |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 200 | 46 | 30 |
| 2020 | 216 | 52 | 31 |
| 2021 | 237 | 55 | 35 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 257

**(b)** (a) Births exceed deaths every year, so r is positive.

**(c)** (i) Numbers will keep rising at first, but the pond has **limited food and space**, so growth will **slow** (deceleration) and the population will level off near the **carrying capacity** — **logistic (S-shaped) growth**, not unlimited exponential growth.

**OR** (ii) With **no immigration or emigration**, changes in numbers are due only to **births and deaths**, so the birth and death rates measured give the true **intrinsic rate of increase** of the population.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** $237 + 55 - 35 = 257$.

**(b)** With no migration, growth depends on births exceeding deaths — option (a).

**(c)** (i) Logistic levelling.

(ii) Only B and D act.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Why was it important that the pond was closed to migration?

answer.model_answer_md: With **no immigration or emigration**, changes in numbers are due only to **births and deaths**, so the birth and death rates measured give the true **intrinsic rate of increase** of the population.

questions.passage_md:
On a rocky shore, 60 lower-shore plots were cleared. In half of the experiment the larger barnacle Balanus was allowed to settle; in the other half it was kept out. After a year, the number of plots in which the small barnacle Chthamalus had survived was recorded.

| Treatment | Plots with surviving Chthamalus (out of 60) |
|---|---|
| Balanus present | 12 |
| Balanus removed | 46 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 76.7 %

**(b)** (b) Balanus out-competes Chthamalus on the lower shore.

**(c)** (i) It is **competitive release**: the inferior competitor **expands** into areas from which the **superior competitor** had excluded it. This resembles **Connell’s** experiments with barnacles on the rocky coast of **Scotland**.

**OR** (ii) Two barnacle species competing for the **same space** on the lower shore **cannot coexist**: the **superior** Balanus **eliminates** most Chthamalus, just as Gause found that one *Paramecium* species excluded the other.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** $\dfrac{46}{60} \times 100 = 76.7$ percent.

**(b)** Chthamalus survives well there only when its competitor is absent — option (b).

**(c)** (i) Competitive release; Connell.

(ii) Exclusion of inferior competitor.

children.stem_md: In what percentage of plots did Chthamalus survive when Balanus was removed?
Chthamalus survived in only 20 percent of plots with Balanus. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text_md: Chthamalus cannot tolerate the lower shore at all.
Balanus out-competes Chthamalus on the lower shore.
Balanus is a mutualist of Chthamalus.
The two barnacles do not interact.

children.solution_md: Chthamalus survives well there only when its competitor is absent — option (b).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Name the phenomenon shown when Balanus is removed, and the scientist whose work this resembles.

answer.model_answer_md: It is **competitive release**: the inferior competitor **expands** into areas from which the **superior competitor** had excluded it. This resembles **Connell’s** experiments with barnacles on the rocky coast of **Scotland**.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): How does this experiment support Gause’s competitive exclusion principle?

answer.model_answer_md: Two barnacle species competing for the **same space** on the lower shore **cannot coexist**: the **superior** Balanus **eliminates** most Chthamalus, just as Gause found that one *Paramecium* species excluded the other.
